1 Introduction

Microbial communities are ubiquitous across diverse ecosystems. However, traditional pure culture methods capture only a small fraction of the microorganisms present, with early estimates suggesting that approximately 0.1–1% of environmental microbes can be cultivated under standard laboratory conditions (Chen et al., 2005). Consequently, the vast majority of microorganisms remain poorly characterized. This limitation constrains comprehensive exploration of microbial diversity and function. Metagenomics overcomes this cultivation dependency by directly analyzing the total genetic material recovered from environmental samples, enabling the characterization of community composition and the inference of the functional potential of microbial communities.

In metagenomic studies, high-throughput sequencing generates a large number of sequencing reads derived from mixed microbial populations. After assembly into longer contiguous sequences (contigs), accurately assigning these sequences to their genomes of origin remains a major challenge in the analysis of complex microbial communities. To address this problem, binning techniques have been developed that apply computational methods to group contigs into clusters representing draft genomes, commonly referred to as metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Binning has therefore become a core approach for reconstructing genomes from metagenomic data and for investigating the genetic characteristics and metabolic potential of previously uncultured microorganisms.

The core principle of binning lies in utilizing intrinsic sequence features (such as GC content, k-mer frequency) and differences in coverage depth to identify and group sequences derived from the same or similar microorganisms within mixed metagenomic data (Sedlar et al., 2024). The typical workflow starts with the acquisition and quality control of metagenomic sequencing data, followed by sequence assembly to generate longer contigs. Subsequently, binning algorithms (e.g., tools based on sequence composition, abundance, or a combination of both) cluster these contigs into distinct "bins," each theoretically representing the genome of an individual microorganism. The quality of these bins is then evaluated and refined based on metrics like completeness and contamination rate, ultimately yielding high-quality MAGs for downstream analysis.

Binning technology has greatly advanced research in microbial ecology, medicine, and environmental science. In human health, for instance, binning enables in-depth analysis of the composition and function of gut microbial communities, revealing their close association with human disease and health (Qin et al., 2010). In environmental science, binning has helped scientists discover and characterize numerous unknown microorganisms in extreme environments like soil and oceans, uncovering their key metabolic potential in global biogeochemical cycles (such as carbon and nitrogen cycles) and novel biocatalysts. Furthermore, integrated with studies like metabolomics, MAGs derived from binning facilitate the elucidation of complex interaction mechanisms within microbial communities and with their environment.

With the continued advancement of long-read sequencing technologies and computational methods, including recent efforts to integrate high-throughput long-read sequencing with deep learning approaches (Hon et al., 2025), the accuracy and applicability of metagenomic binning are expected to improve further. These developments will enhance the reconstruction of high-quality genomes from complex microbial communities and facilitate the exploration of previously uncharacterized microbial diversity.

2 Library Construction and Sequencing

The genomic DNA was randomly sheared into shorter fragments. The obtained fragments were then end-repaired, A-tailed, and further ligated with sequencing adapters. The resulting fragments with adapters were size selected and PCR amplified, unless otherwise specified as PCR-free, before proceeding for purification.

The experimental procedures of DNA library preparation are shown in Figure 2.1:


Figure 2.1 Workflow of library construction

The library was quantified using Qubit and qPCR, and the size distribution was detected with a fragment analyzer. Quantified libraries were pooled and sequenced according to the effective library concentration and required data amount.

3 Bioinformatics Analysis Pipeline

The raw sequencing data (Raw Data) contained a certain proportion of low-quality reads. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of subsequent bioinformatic analysis, quality control and host sequence filtering were first performed on the Raw Data to obtain valid data (Clean Data). Based on the quality-controlled Clean Data from each sample, a de novo assembly strategy for second-generation sequencing data was employed for assembly, yielding scaffolds (Li et al., 2015).

The binning process was performed on individual samples using MetaWRAP, a tool that integrates three mainstream binning software packages: MaxBin2, MetaBAT2, and CONCOCT (Uritskiy et al., 2018). First, bwa-index was used to build the index for the assembled contigs. Then, the paired-end reads from the sample were aligned to this index. The alignment results were sorted and compressed using samtools, while statistics on library insert size were also collected. After MaxBin2, MetaBAT2, and CONCOCT completed fragment binning with default settings, a final binning folder was created, which contained the formatted bin fasta files.

Based on the results from MetaBAT2, MaxBin2, and CONCOCT, the optimal bins were integrated using the bin_refinement module of MetaWRAP. Subsequently, for the refined binning results, dRep was employed to perform clustering and deduplication of bins across all samples (Olm et al., 2017). CheckM was then run to evaluate the completeness and contamination level of each bin (Parks et al., 2015). Finally, GTDB-Tk was used to perform taxonomic annotation of the bins (Chaumeil et al., 2019).

Subsequently, gene prediction for each bin was performed using Prokka (Seemann, 2014), and functional annotation was conducted on the predicted protein sequences. The functional annotation employed multiple methods, including dbCAN (for carbohydrate-active enzymes), eggNOG-mapper (for comprehensive annotation based on orthologous groups, encompassing Gene Ontology terms, Enzyme Commission numbers, KEGG pathways, and protein domain predictions), VFDB (for virulence factors), CARD (for antibiotic resistance genes), and BacMet2 (for metal and biocide resistance genes).

Additionally, to investigate the distribution of mobile genetic elements (MGEs) within the microbial community and their potential association with the horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factors (VFs), a specialized MGE annotation was performed on the dereplicated MAGs. The primary tool employed was geNomad (Camargo et al., 2024), which utilizes deep neural networks for efficient identification of viruses (including prophages), plasmids, and composite MGEs. This analysis was supplemented with MobileElementFinder (Johansson et al., 2021) for the detection of elements such as insertion sequences and transposons. This integrated strategy enabled a comprehensive assessment of MGE abundance and functional load, providing insights for understanding microbial evolutionary dynamics and resistance dissemination mechanisms.

4 Analysis Results


4.1 Sequencing data processing

The raw sequencing data underwent preprocessing, which included the following steps: paired reads were removed if either read in the pair contained adapter sequences; if either read contained more than 50% of bases with low quality (Q≤5); or if either read contained over 10% of N bases. For samples with potential host contamination, reads were aligned to the host genome using Bowtie2 (by default), and sequences likely originating from the host were filtered out (Karlsson et al., 2012; Karlsson et al., 2013; Scher et al., 2013), thereby obtaining clean data for subsequent analysis. All the above processing steps were applied to both read 1 and read 2. The statistical results of the sequencing data preprocessing are presented in the table below.

4.3 Binning

The binning module integrated three mainstream metagenomic binning software tools using MetaWRAP: MaxBin2, MetaBAT2, and CONCOCT (Uritskiy et al., 2018). First, the metagenomic assembly results were indexed using bwa-index, and then paired-end reads from any number of samples were aligned to the assembly. The alignment results were sorted and compressed using samtools, and statistical data on library insert sizes (including mean and standard deviation) were collected. Next, the jgi_summarize_bam_contig_depths function of MetaBAT2 was used to generate a contig abundance table, which was then converted into input formats suitable for each binning software. MaxBin2, MetaBAT2, and CONCOCT performed contig binning under default settings, ultimately generating a bin folder containing formatted bin FASTA files, facilitating subsequent bin-based extended analyses.

4.4 Refinement of Bins

The Bin_refinement module employed a hybrid approach to integrate two or three bin sets obtained from different software (or the same software with different parameters) into a single, improved bin set (Uritskiy et al., 2018). First, binning_refiner was used to generate hybrid bins from every possible combination. Given three bin sets, A, B, and C, binning_refiner produced the following hybrid sets: AB, BC, AC, and ABC. CheckM was then run to evaluate the completeness and contamination of bins within each bin set (the three original sets and the four hybrid sets) (Parks et al., 2015). Subsequently, the bin sets were iteratively compared, and each pair of bin sets was merged into an improved bin set. To achieve this, identical bins in two bin sets were identified based on at least 80% overlap in genome length, and the best bin was determined according to the bin with the higher score. The scoring function was defined as S = completeness - 5 × contamination. After all bin sets were merged into a final bin set, a dereplication feature removed any duplicate contigs: if a contig was present in multiple bins, it was deleted from all bins and retained only in the highest-scoring bin. CheckM was then run again to evaluate the final bin set, generating a final report file containing completeness, contamination, and other statistics produced by CheckM for each bin. Additionally, completeness and contamination ranking plots were generated to assess the success of the Bin_refinement module and compare its output with the quality of the original bins.

4.5 Genome Quality Assessment

After optimization by the Bin_refinement module, dRep was used to cluster and dereplicate the refined bins in order to integrate the bin results from all samples and remove potential redundancy (Olm et al., 2017). In this step, an initial genome-wide similarity screening was first performed using Mash. Representative bins were then selected based on the ANI (Average Nucleotide Identity) threshold (default 95%) and CheckM quality scores (including completeness and contamination). Finally, a project-wide, non-redundant set of MAGs was generated. This ensured the uniqueness and high quality of the bins, prevented redundant representations from affecting downstream analyses, and provided a reliable foundation for subsequent final quality assessment.

For the bins after dereplication, CheckM was used as a key tool in metagenomic analysis to evaluate genome quality (binning results). It estimated genome completeness and contamination by identifying specific marker genes (Parks et al., 2015). Its core advantage lay in its ability to use lineage-specific marker gene sets for evaluation, based on the genome's position in the phylogenetic tree. This made the assessment results more accurate, particularly suitable for the analysis of MAGs from complex microbial communities.

4.6 GTDB Taxonomic Classification


4.6.1 Result of Taxonomic Classification

GTDB-Tk (Genome Taxonomy Database Toolkit) was used as a tool for standardized taxonomic annotation of bacterial and archaeal genomes based on the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) (Chaumeil et al., 2019). Its core advantage lay in its use of whole-genome phylogenetic analysis rather than traditional 16S rRNA gene sequences, providing a more objective and accurate taxonomic framework. This approach was particularly suitable for the taxonomic classification of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) obtained from binning.

classification: Taxonomic lineage in GTDB (Genome Taxonomy Database) standard format
closest_genome_reference: Closest reference genome ID, typically an NCBI Assembly GCF_ or GCA_ ID, representing the known reference genome most similar to the user's genome (based on ANI or other similarity metrics)

4.6.2 MAGs Statistical Analysis

In the statistical analysis of MAGs, the number of MAGs annotated to different taxa at the phylum level was quantified. A donut chart (panel a) was generated to illustrate the distribution of the annotation results, clearly displaying the counts and relative proportions of the various taxonomic groups. Additionally, a bar chart (panel b) was constructed to showcase the classification rates of MAGs across multiple taxonomic levels. In this visualization, blue segments represent the proportion of MAGs successfully annotated to the corresponding taxon, while gray segments indicate the proportion of unclassified MAGs. White annotations within the bars provide the precise number and percentage of MAGs assigned to specific classifications at each hierarchical level. The results are presented as follows:


Figure 4.1 MAGs Quantity Statistics: Donut Chart (a) and MAGs Classification Statistics: Bar Chart (b)

Result file directory:

MAGs Classification Statistics Chart: Result/03.Binning/GTDB/gtdb_taxonomic_classification_rate.png

Combined Figure: Result/03.Binning/GTDB/gtdb_combine.png


4.7 Gene Prediction

Gene prediction was a critical step in metagenomic analysis, aimed at identifying protein-coding genes (CDSs) and non-coding RNAs (such as rRNA, tRNA, and tmRNA) from assembled sequences (e.g., contigs or scaffolds) or binning results, thereby providing foundational data for downstream functional annotation and metabolic analysis. Prokka was a rapid prokaryotic genome annotation tool, specifically designed for efficiently predicting and annotating bacterial or archaeal genomes (Seemann, 2014). Its core methodology included: using Prodigal for ab initio open reading frame (ORF) prediction to identify CDSs; incorporating tools like RNAmmer and Aragorn to detect non-coding RNAs such as rRNA, tRNA, and tmRNA; and integrating homology-based alignments (e.g., BLAST searches against Swiss-Prot or UniProt) to enhance annotation accuracy.

4.8 Functional Annotation

Functional annotation was a downstream key step in metagenomic analysis, aimed at performing functional prediction and classification on the protein sequences predicted from each bin, thereby revealing the functional diversity, metabolic pathways, and ecological roles of microbial genomes. By integrating these annotation methods, multi-dimensional functional insights were provided to support subsequent pathway abundance analysis and ecological modeling, making this approach particularly suitable for the study of MAGs in complex microbial communities.


4.8.1 dbCAN Carbohydrate-Active Enzyme Annotation

dbCAN (Carbohydrate-active enzyme ANnotation) was a web server and toolkit specifically designed for the automated annotation of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) (Zheng et al., 2023). The primary goal of dbCAN was to efficiently identify, classify, and predict the functions of CAZyme genes in genomic or metagenomic sequences by integrating multiple computational methods, thereby helping researchers elucidate the role of microorganisms in carbohydrate metabolism, which was particularly useful in metagenomic analysis.

dbCAN relied on several core databases, including the dbCAN CAZyme domain HMM database (used for HMMER searches, containing hidden Markov models for hundreds of CAZyme families and subfamilies), the CAZy database (used for DIAMOND similarity searches, covering millions of CAZyme sequences), and the dbCAN-sub HMM database (used for subfamily annotation and substrate prediction). Its annotation methodology primarily included three approaches: (1) HMMER searches for domain annotation of CAZyme families; (2) DIAMOND searches against the CAZy database for BLAST-like alignments; and (3) HMMER searches for subfamily-level CAZyme annotation, which inferred EC numbers and glycan substrates. By combining these methods, comprehensive annotation results were provided.

Using dbCAN for annotation revealed the distribution and functional diversity of enzymes related to carbohydrate degradation, synthesis, and transport within microbial communities. This contributed to understanding carbon cycling processes in ecosystems.

Gene ID: Protein sequence ID
EC#: EC number (Enzyme Commission number), indicating the enzyme's classification and catalytic activity (e.g., 3.2.1.68 represents a specific hydrolase), inferred from the CAZy database. If empty ("-"), no reliable enzyme annotation is available.
dbCAN_hmm: CAZyme family hits from the HMMER tool (e.g., GH177(3-309)), including the family and domain positions. Multiple hits are separated by "+".
dbCAN_sub: Substrate specificity prediction results from the dbCAN-sub tool (e.g., GH109_e7(4-147)), including substrate prediction and positions. "-" indicates no result.
DIAMOND: Hit results from DIAMOND BLAST against the CAZy database (e.g., GT2), representing the best family match from similarity searches.
ofTools: Number of tools supporting this annotation (HMMER, dbCAN_sub, DIAMOND). A higher value indicates greater reliability (e.g., ≥2 suggests high quality).
Recommend Results: Recommended final annotation result, based on multi-tool consensus (e.g., GH109_e7), integrating tool hits and prioritizing high-quality predictions. Multiple results are separated by "|".



Result file directory: result/05.MAG_Annotation/dbcan/dbcan.stat.tsv

Based on the carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations for each bin, the annotated families were classified into six major functional categories: Auxiliary Activities (AA), Carbohydrate-Binding Modules (CBM), Carbohydrate Esterases (CE), Glycoside Hydrolases (GH), GlycosylTransferases (GT), and Polysaccharide Lyases (PL). The number of genes in each category was counted, and a bar chart was generated for visualization.

4.8.2 Orthologous Groups Comprehensive Functional Annotation

eggNOG-mapper (evolutionary genealogy of genes: Non-supervised Orthologous Groups - mapper) was a tool specifically designed for rapid whole-genome functional annotation through orthology assignment (Cantalapiedra et al., 2021). Based on precomputed orthologous groups and phylogenies from the eggNOG database, it transferred functional information from fine-grained orthologs, thereby avoiding the low precision often associated with traditional homology searches (such as BLAST) caused by functional divergence among paralogs.

The core database relied upon by eggNOG-mapper was eggNOG 5.0 (http://eggnog5.embl.de/ ), a resource of precomputed orthologous groups containing phylogenetic and functional information for millions of sequences. It was also linked with other databases, such as InterPro, for domain predictions. The output included various types of functional annotations: (1) Orthologous Groups (OGs) and COG/KOG classifications for functional descriptions and evolutionary analysis; (2) Gene Ontology (GO) terms for annotating biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components; (3) Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers for enzyme classification; (4) KEGG pathways and modules for predicting metabolic pathways and reaction networks; and (5) protein domain predictions, such as Pfam domains.

Regarding its application in metagenomic functional annotation, by performing orthology-based annotation on bin-derived proteins, eggNOG-mapper revealed the functional diversity, metabolic potential, and social interactions of microbial communities. For example, it identified key pathways such as carbon and nitrogen cycling or antibiotic synthesis in environmental, gut, or soil metagenomes. Particularly in high-throughput sequencing projects, it was instrumental in understanding the functional dynamics of ecosystems.

COG_category: COG (Clusters of Orthologous Groups) functional category code, using a single letter to indicate the broad functional classification of the protein (e.g., "E" for Amino acid transport and metabolism, "S" for Unknown function). Assigned based on the best orthologous group match at an appropriate taxonomic level. "-" indicates no COG category assigned.
Description: Textual description of the predicted protein function, derived from the best-matching orthologous group (OG) in eggNOG. Provides a human-readable summary (e.g., "Pasta domain protein"). "-" indicates no description available.
GOs: Gene Ontology terms, separated by commas (e.g., "GO:0000166,GO:0003674"). These describe the protein's molecular function, biological process, and cellular component, propagated from orthology-based annotations. "-" indicates no GO terms assigned.
KEGG_ko: KEGG Orthology (KO) identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "ko:K12132"). KO terms represent orthologous genes or proteins associated with KEGG pathways and reactions. "-" indicates no KO assigned.
KEGG_Pathway: KEGG pathway identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "ko:00300,ko:01100"). Indicates the metabolic or signaling pathways (e.g., Fructose and mannose metabolism) in which the protein is involved. "-" indicates no pathway assigned.
KEGG_Module: KEGG module identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "M00016,M00525"). Modules represent functional units or sub-pathways within a pathway. "-" indicates no module assigned.
KEGG_Reaction: KEGG reaction identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "R00451"). Describes specific enzymatic reactions catalyzed by the protein. "-" indicates no reaction assigned.
BRITE: KEGG BRITE hierarchy identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "ko00000,ko01000"). BRITE is KEGG's hierarchical classification system for functionally categorizing genes, compounds, and pathways, providing a structure from broad to specific levels (e.g., ko00000 represents KEGG Orthology). It helps in understanding the protein's context within larger biological systems. "-" indicates no BRITE assigned.
KEGG_TC: KEGG Transporter Classification identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "4.A.2.1"). These classify transporters (e.g., ion pumps, channels, or carriers) based on the TCDB (Transporter Classification Database) system (e.g., 4.A.2.1 represents a PTS system). It is specifically for describing protein transport functions. "-" indicates no KEGG_TC assigned.
KEGG_rclass: KEGG reaction class identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "RC00299"). Reaction classes group similar reactions based on chemical transformations. "-" indicates no reaction class assigned.
PFAMs: PFAM domain identifiers, separated by commas (e.g., "PASTA"). Indicates conserved protein domains or motifs detected in the query sequence. "-" indicates no PFAM domains assigned.

4.8.3 CARD Antibiotic Resistance Functional Annotation

CARD (Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database) was a bioinformatics database focused on the rigorous curation and annotation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), their products, and associated phenotypes (Alcock et al., 2023). Central to CARD was the Antibiotic Resistance Ontology (ARO), an ontological framework used to organize resistance determinants, antibiotics, and related data.

The core components relied upon by CARD included: (1) the ARO ontology, which standardized the classification and relationship modeling of resistance genes, encompassing 8,582 ontology terms; (2) a reference sequence database, containing 6,442 reference sequences and 4,480 SNPs; (3) 6,480 AMR detection models used for homology- and SNP-based predictions; and (4) Resistome & Variants (CARD-R), which provided in silico resistome predictions for 414 pathogens, 24,291 chromosomes, 172,216 whole genome assemblies (WGS), and prevalence statistics of AMR genes in pathogens, genomes, and plasmids. Its annotation methodology was primarily implemented through the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI) tool, which included: (1) homology-based searches using DIAMOND or BLAST-like alignment against CARD reference sequences to identify ARGs; (2) SNP models for detecting known resistance mutations; and (3) integration of the ARO for classification and mechanism prediction, employing threshold settings such as perfect, strict, or loose matches.

By annotating bin-derived proteins with RGI, CARD revealed the distribution of antibiotic resistance genes, mechanistic diversity, and potential risks within microbial communities. For example, it identified β-lactamases or tetracycline resistance genes in soil, wastewater, or gut metagenomes. This contributed to understanding the ecological dissemination and evolutionary dynamics of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

Best_Hit_ARO: Best Hit Antibiotic Resistance Ontology, indicating the name of the best-matching resistance gene ontology (ARO) term from the CARD database. This represents the optimal ARG match selected by RGI based on alignment scores (e.g., bitscore).
Drug Class: Drug class, indicating the category of antibiotic or disinfectant associated with the ARG. It describes the broad type of resistance based on CARD's classification system.
Antibiotic: Specific antibiotic, indicating the precise drug or compound targeted by the ARG. This column specifies the exact antibiotic against which the resistance mechanism acts, based on CARD's drug-resistance associations.



Result file directory: result/05.MAG_Annotation/CARD/CARD.stat.tsv


4.8.4 BacMet2 Metal Resistance

BacMet2 (Antibacterial Biocide and Metal Resistance Genes Database) was a bioinformatics database focused on the curation and annotation of bacterial resistance genes to metals and antibacterial biocides (such as disinfectants and antiseptics) (Pal et al., 2014). This database was built upon an extensive review of the scientific literature, providing manually curated content and linking to related resources such as antibiotic resistance databases.

The primary purpose of BacMet2 was to offer a high-quality, easy-to-use resource for identifying and classifying bacterial resistance genes, which was particularly useful for revealing the adaptive mechanisms of microorganisms under environmental stress. It integrated experimentally confirmed resistance genes and their products, aiding researchers in exploring the evolutionary dynamics of resistance transmission, especially concerning metals (e.g., copper, zinc, mercury) and biocides (e.g., quaternary ammonium compounds, triclosan). BacMet2 was organized into two core databases: (1) an experimentally confirmed database containing 753 genes (550 of chromosomal origin and 203 from plasmids/transposons), covering 268 biocide resistance genes, 420 metal resistance genes, and 65 genes conferring resistance to both; and (2) a predicted database containing 155,512 potential resistance genes based on sequence similarity. These genes were associated with 111 compounds across 43 chemical classes, including 58 antibacterial biocides, 23 metals, and 30 other compounds.

Regarding its application in metagenomic functional annotation, by performing similarity-based annotation on bin-derived proteins, BacMet2 revealed the distribution of metal and biocide resistance genes, their mechanistic diversity, and ecological significance within microbial communities. For example, it identified mercury reductases or copper efflux pump genes in soil, wastewater, or industrial environment metagenomes. This contributed to understanding the horizontal transfer of resistance genes and the impacts of environmental pollution.

Compound: Associated compound, indicating the resistance-related substance or compound associated with the gene (e.g., Triclosan [class: Phenolic compounds]), including its classification (e.g., class: Phenolic compounds). This describes the specific metal, disinfectant, or compound targeted by the resistance mechanism.
NCBI_annotation: NCBI annotation, indicating the functional description from the NCBI database (e.g., enoyl-acyl-carrier-protein), providing the biological function or protein description of the gene.

4.8.5 VFDB Virulence Factor Functional Annotation

VFDB (Virulence Factor Database) was a bioinformatics database dedicated to the curation, classification, and annotation of bacterial virulence factors (VFs), providing virulence-related knowledge for various bacterial pathogens (Chen et al., 2005). \\EN

The main purpose of VFDB was to offer a unified and easy-to-use resource for the identification and analysis of bacterial virulence factors, which was particularly useful for revealing the pathogenic mechanisms and evolutionary dynamics of pathogens. It integrated experimentally confirmed virulence genes and their products, helping researchers explore infection processes, host interactions, and potential therapeutic targets. VFDB was divided into a core dataset (focusing on VFs from known pathogens) and a comparative dataset (covering homologs across all bacterial genomes), containing thousands of reference sequences, classifications, and literature citations. Its core components included: (1) a manually curated reference sequence database based on literature review and experimental validation; (2) a universal classification scheme (introduced in 2022) that categorized VFs into offensive, defensive, regulatory, and nonspecific classes; (3) an antivirulence module (added in 2025) that included compound structures, targets, and mechanism information; and (4) phylogenetic information linking to hundreds of pathogens and millions of sequences.

Regarding its application in metagenomic functional annotation, by performing similarity-based annotation on bin-derived proteins, VFDB revealed the distribution of virulence factors, their mechanistic diversity, and pathogenic potential within microbial communities. For example, it identified invasins or toxin genes in gut, environmental, or clinical metagenomes. This contributed to understanding pathogen transmission, host-microbe interactions, and emerging infection risks.

VF_id: Virulence factor ID, indicating the unique identifier for a virulence factor in the VFDB (e.g., VF1157), used to reference specific virulence-related genes or mechanisms.
VF_name: Virulence factor name, indicating the descriptive name of the virulence factor (e.g., C3610 or Flagella), providing a human-readable summary of the virulence factor.
VFCID: Virulence factor category ID, indicating the category identifier for the virulence factor in the VFDB (e.g., VFC0001), used to classify the functional group of the virulence factor.
Vfcategory: Virulence factor category, indicating the functional category of the virulence factor (e.g., Adherence), describing the broad type of virulence mechanism (such as adherence, motility, or metabolic factors).



Result file directory: result/05.MAG_Annotation/VFDB/VFDB.stat.tsv


4.8.6 Mobile Genetic Elements(MGEs) Annotation

Mobile Genetic Elements (MGEs) referred to DNA segments capable of moving within a bacterial genome or transferring between bacteria. They primarily included plasmids, viruses/phages (including prophages), insertion sequences (IS), transposons, and integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs). These elements were key drivers of microbial evolution and the horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factors (VFs), attracting significant attention in metagenomic research.

In this study, geNomad was employed as the primary tool for MGE identification (Camargo et al., 2024). geNomad was a comprehensive framework based on deep neural networks and marker genes, capable of efficiently detecting and classifying viral and plasmid sequences simultaneously. It demonstrated state-of-the-art accuracy and sensitivity on metagenomic assembled sequences, including MAGs. Its core functionality relied on built-in protein profile databases (covering 227,897 virus, plasmid, and chromosome-specific markers) and neural network models. Operating in an end-to-end manner, it performed gene prediction, classification, and functional annotation on input sequences, outputting information including plasmid_score/virus_score, counts of hallmark genes, marker enrichment, and the presence of potential conjugation genes and AMR genes. To complement the detection of elements such as insertion sequences and transposons, MobileElementFinder was further utilized (Johansson et al., 2021). This tool specialized in the rapid identification of IS, composite transposons, and their genetic context, performing BLAST-based alignments against the MGEdb database to provide detailed information on element location, orientation, and type.

Regarding its application in metagenomic functional annotation, the systematic identification and classification of MGEs within bins revealed the potential for horizontal gene transfer within microbial communities, the distribution of vectors carrying ARGs and VFs, and associated dissemination risks. For example, this approach identified conjugative plasmids or prophages harboring resistance genes in environmental, gut, or clinical samples. This contributed to understanding the ecological mechanisms of resistance transmission, microbial evolutionary dynamics, and the origins of emerging resistance threats.

topology: Sequence topology (describing the terminal repeat characteristics of the contig, e.g., "No terminal repeats" indicates no terminal repeats, "ITR" indicates inverted terminal repeats, "DTR" indicates direct terminal repeats; circular plasmids are often associated with ITR/DTR, supporting potential circularity).
plasmid_score: Plasmid prediction score (plasmid probability calculated by the neural network model, ranging from 0 to 1; a higher score indicates that the sequence is more similar to known plasmids in composition and features, with scores >0.9 typically considered high-confidence candidates).
fdr: False Discovery Rate corrected value (statistical significance after multiple testing correction; "NA" indicates insufficient sample size for correction or no significant statistics).
conjugation_genes: Detected conjugation genes (semicolon-separated list of genes, e.g., T_virB series; these are genes related to the Type IV secretion system (T4SS), supporting potential conjugative properties and providing key evidence for MGE horizontal transfer).
amr_genes: Detected antibiotic resistance genes (semicolon-separated gene IDs, e.g., ARG identifiers starting with NF from geNomad's built-in database; indicates potential resistance genes carried in the sequence, which can be cross-validated with databases such as CARD).

topology: Sequence topology (describing viral candidate features, e.g., "Provirus" indicates a prophage integrated into the host genome, "No terminal repeats" indicates no terminal repeats, potentially suggesting a linear virus or incomplete sequence; prophages are common MGE types in bacterial MAGs).
genetic_code: Genetic code (11 represents the bacterial/archaeal genetic code table, confirming the prokaryotic origin of the sequence).
virus_score: Virus prediction score (viral probability calculated by the neural network model, ranging from 0 to 1; a higher score indicates that the sequence is more similar to known viruses/phages in composition and features, with scores >0.9 typically considered high-confidence candidates).
n_hallmarks: Number of detected viral hallmark genes (virus-specific marker genes, such as capsid, terminase, etc.; a count ≥1 serves as core evidence for reliable virus/prophage identification, with ≥2–3 providing strong support).
marker_enrichment: Enrichment score for viral marker genes (a higher score indicates significant enrichment of virus-like marker genes in the sequence, with values >5–10 typically supporting high-confidence identification).

MGE_type: Mobile genetic element type (primarily includes Insertion Sequence, Composite Transposon, Unit Transposon, or ICE (Integrative and Conjugative Element), reflecting the structural category of the element).
Mge_name: Mobile genetic element specific name (based on standardized nomenclature from the MGEdb database, e.g., ISTfo1, indicating a known insertion sequence family or subtype, aiding in tracing the element's origin and evolutionary relationships).
Identity (Query/Template): Identity percentage between the query and template sequences (indicates the nucleic acid similarity between the detected element sequence and the database reference template; a higher percentage suggests stronger homology, with values >70% typically considered reliable matches).
HSP: High-scoring Segment Pair length (formatted as "query coverage length / template length", reflecting the coverage of the best matching segment in the BLAST alignment, used to evaluate alignment quality and completeness).
Contig: Name of the contig containing the element (indicates the specific assembled sequence fragment to which the mobile genetic element is localized, facilitating subsequent sequence extraction and visualization).
Position_in_contig: Coordinates of the element on the contig (formatted as "start position..end position", using 1-based coordinates, indicating the precise interval of the element within the contig, which can be used for downstream gene context analysis or visualization).
